what: The explanatory content of the lane’s private field map (round5/dashboard/r310-field-map.html, state at 01:56 UTC on 25 Nov 2026), rebuilt as data with a needle per sentence and number: the ladder of R(3,k), the nested structure, the slack, the reach of methods, the three phantoms, the funnel and its tools, six open questions, a glossary, the lane’s own map of strata brought up to the ledger’s last entries, and the field map’s forecasts, kept apart as forecasts.

phantoms.name: The one-view phantom
phantoms.what: Take one real graph on 30 points and pretend it is what every one of the 40 points sees outside its neighbours. Every count made from a single point is then consistent, at any depth.
phantoms.why: It forgets that the views of two points overlap and must agree where they do. This is why ten methods stop at 43. Sharper methods are fooled the same way by a blend of about seven real graphs.

phantoms.name: The pair phantom
phantoms.what: A table of how many pairs of each kind exist, with every pair consistent in itself. It satisfies 35 exact equations in whole numbers.
phantoms.why: Pairs are never asked to agree on a third point. The same phantom, one level up. Found at the stratum with largest codegree 4.

phantoms.name: The scale phantom
phantoms.what: A real graph with the same proportions as ours, 320 points with 72 neighbours each, where every neighbourhood is a largest unconnected set. Built from a 2010 paper’s recipe.
phantoms.why: Any argument that only uses ratios would exclude it too, and it exists. So ratios alone can never work.

fourth: Real graphs on 40 points obey every local rule (9 neighbours each, no triangle, 1 to 3 shared neighbours) and still contain ten unconnected points. So nothing built from local rules alone can finish the proof.
not_fooled: Three kinds of input survive all three phantoms: an exact small Ramsey number applied to a region of the graph (18 points untouched by 4 chosen ones must contain 6 unconnected, since R(3,6) = 18); whole-number constraints; and statements that force two or more points’ views to agree.
funnel: from a paper, an agent, or from the operator
ruled by the words written before the run
bench: The test bench is the pair 22 and 23. At 22 points ten graphs of the regular kind exist; at 23 none does; and counting leaves slack there, as it does at 40. A method must say “possible” at 22 and “impossible” at 23 without being handed the list of smaller graphs.

tools.t: GPT sessions started from this Mac. Each gets one bounded task and a gate. They read everything, write only in their own folder.
The second programs: re-derive a result from the written mathematics before opening the first program’s output. Also the paper scouts.
Every graph at the solved rungs, on disk (477,142 at one of them). A method that “excludes” a graph that exists is wrong.
Every machine refutation is replayed by two independent checkers before it counts.
What counts as pass or fail is written and timestamped before the run, then ruled by its own words.
A row before any work. Dead only with the number that killed it. Alive only after a second program.
End of the funnel: a surviving lemma becomes a decidable object over a pinned catalogue.
8 cores, no rented machines. Any route ending in thousands of CPU-hours is out by rule.

questions.text: Ten regular graphs exist on 22 points; none on 23. Every count we can write is satisfied on both sides. Something that is not a count separates them. At 18 points the answer is now known: the counts are forced to a single table, every local piece is a real graph, and still the pieces cannot be assembled into one graph, even ignoring the ten-set rule. At 23 they can be assembled, so something more breaks there. Name it, and it is the thing to carry up to 40.

questions.q: What is the smallest statement about two views agreeing?
questions.text: Each point sees 30 others outside its neighbours. Two joined points share 22 of those. A proof must use that overlap. Listing all overlaps is the brute force we ruled out; a single inequality about them is what is missing.

In every solved case, a graph at the limit contains unconnected sets whose untouched parts are a fixed 8-point graph, then a 5-cycle, then a single line. All 477,142 graphs one rung down do. At 40 only the last step is proved. Counting cannot prove the next; it would need 45 points.

questions.q: Is the regular case the whole problem?
questions.text: In every catalogue, whenever a graph exists, one with the maximum possible number of lines exists too. If that held at 40, a counterexample would exist only if a 9-regular one did, and half the map would vanish. No proof is known at any size.

questions.q: Can rigid spots be forced, then chained?
questions.text: When a region is exactly as large as a Ramsey number allows, its shape is one of a handful. One such spot (three points fully joined to four) fixes seven whole neighbourhoods. The open question is whether such spots must exist, and whether two of them can coexist.

questions.q: Where do the 13 extra lines go?
questions.text: Each untouched part has 13 more lines than the leanest possible graph of its size. The leanest graphs are understood, built from a few patterns. Nothing is known 13 lines above them. A description of what the surplus must look like would be new mathematics.

glossary.def: Points with no line between any two of them. Mathematicians say “independent set”.

The graph on the 40 vertices joining two unjoined vertices that have exactly 5 common neighbours.
The regular cases already closed that are built like the case at 40: (6,18), (7,23), (8,28). Every path is asked first to close them without the catalogue of the level below.
Code written from the statement alone by another session, without reading the first program; “independent” on this page means that and nothing more.

strata.text: 283 of the 519 distributions left after five integer rays are excluded at published edge floors, every one by two programs: at most two vertices of degree 6 (two routes), then (0,16,0,24), (0,4,28,8) and a degree-7 floor of 109 with its 8 keys. 236 survive. The floor 110 is not proved: G31 and G32 closed 30 of its 59 root types, and G33 stopped without a verdict.

strata.what: Regular; no two unjoined vertices share more than 3.
strata.text: Covered by 7 rooted configurations (two programs), none closed. Its local window looks rigid: every symmetric member found is one graph G, which has an independent 10-set. Proved with LRAT: no member other than G has a symmetry of order 5, 7 or a prime ≥ 11, a fixed-point-free involution, or an involution fixing exactly two, four or six vertices; the involution types 2^14 1^12 and loopless 2^13 1^14 remain (W1j stopped without a verdict); the asymmetric case is priced at 298 core-hours or more and parked.

strata.what: Regular; the largest shared neighbourhood is 4.
strata.text: 69 six-row profiles, 9 closed by short arguments a person can read (two derivations), 60 open. A rigid 2K₂ root is forced at every maximum pair (confirmed), but a real 40-vertex graph satisfies all of its one- and two-point cards.

1,839 + 118 profiles before any exclusion (one session’s count); none excluded. Round 6 took the graph H5 joining two unjoined vertices with exactly 5 common neighbours: in any 9-regular candidate it has no K4, so no K5 (H1, H2: one session’s proofs, two checkers, accepted as reported); its triangles are open (H3 failed).
The three-edge branch: all 23,409 cores excluded under six premises (box 3). The four-edge branch: a 20-core cost pilot only. Five to nine cross-edges: not run.
Excluded: 977,008 configurations, every one refuted; first by Chen’s run, then by ours (box 2).

settled: Also settled: a vertex with 4 or 5 neighbours is impossible; codegree above 7 is impossible; codegree 1 and 2 are excluded (the second conditionally).

forecasts.moves: The lane’s number moves up if something closes the 23-point regular case without the list below it, and again if the same thing bites at 40. It moves down if all three attempts on that case fail the same way.
